newsitem.title: UK: Cautious OPEC wins applause, market expects encore.
newsitem.headline: Cautious OPEC wins applause, market expects encore.

text.p: Oil traders sent a simple but emphatic message on Friday to OPEC ministers preparing for next week's production talks in Vienna: "Leave well alone."

They say the 11 members of the Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) will enjoy an unexpected $30 billion bonus this year and should resist the temptation to raise output when they meet on Wednesday to set 1997 production levels.

"You have to bear in mind that by doing nothing they have succeeded so they'll probably be saying "let's not bother too much here'," said Russell Hill, senior crude trader in London for Austrian oil producer and refiner OMV.

Oil prices have been hovering around their highest levels in more than six years since mid-October amid a bullish cocktail of Middle East tensions, buoyant demand and fear that low heating oil stocks will fall short this winter.
The price has gone well above the most bullish forecasts and has brought in windfall earnings for all oil producers. But it has also raised inflation fears among major consumers.

Although prices have retreated nearly $2 a barrel in recent weeks, traders and analysts believe a rollover of OPEC's self-imposed but widely ignored 25.03 million barrel-per-day (bpd) ceiling will keep them strong well into next year.
"(A rollover) is either neutral to slightly bullish. I believe it's already in the guts of the market but there could be an emotional reaction," said OMV's Hill.

At its last ministerial gathering in June, OPEC left output quotas unchanged for all members bar Iraq, given an extra 800,000 bpd to allow for the much-delayed U.N. oil-for-food sale which has yet to be implemented.
Freezing the ceiling would send a clear and bullish signal that the largest chunk of unused production capacity -- two million bpd in Saudi Arabia -- remains out of bounds for now.

"There are some traders who know nothing else but that Saudi Arabia has a quota of eight million barrels per day, so to some it would be bearish as hell for the Saudis to go up," said Vahan Zanoyan at Washington-based Petroleum Finance Corp (PFC).
Although demand is strong and prices well above 1995 levels, Saudi Arabia, the world's largest oil producer, is not keen to tamper with quotas now, OPEC delegates said.

"There is a logic which says they could raise slightly and get away with it, but if markets fall apart they tend to do so in the Spring and a price of well above $20 is enough for the Saudis," a European oil trader said.
World benchmark Brent crude oil was worth about $23.50 a barrel on Friday, $5 above where it was a year ago.
The high price comes despite the fact that OPEC is pumping about one million bpd above its own ceiling.

OPEC watchers said any move to increase individual allotments or clamp down on cheating within its ranks would spark a row between the few core members who adhere to their quotas -- Saudi Arabia, Kuwait and the United Arab Emirates -- and those who are pumping as much as they can.

"OPEC should roll over because the market is balanced at the moment. Even with cold weather, (supply) tightness will be temporary so any extra OPEC oil would be bearish," said Oysten Berentsen, crude trading head at Norway state oil giant Statoil.

The Paris-based International Energy Agency said earlier this month first quarter 1997 global oil demand would rise 1.8 million bpd year-on-year but rising non-OPEC supply would more than keep pace with growing consumption.
The possibility of a resumption of Iraqi exports for the first time since the Gulf War should also encourage OPEC to plump for a cautious approach, industry observers said.
"If they're not going to do anything when prices are low why should they not be as patient when prices are high?" PFC's Zanoyhan said.
